notes: Hook overclaim corrected: "Two equal masses on three equal springs make a small model of a ship's propulsion shaft" is not in the research. The shaft sources model torsional vibration of shafting as turning inertias on twisting springs (PMC: "ship shafting ... submarine propulsion system shafting"), and a real shaft has many inertias and its own end conditions, not two masses between two fixed walls. Now reads: "Two equal masses on three equal springs shudder in a tangle. A ship's propulsion shaft twists to and fro in the same kind of way, and engineers work it out with the same sums. Which two simple swings hide inside the masses' shudder, and what sets how fast each one goes?" The same sums are backed by Dyrobes and Aalto (notes 7.1): natural frequencies are the square roots of the eigenvalues and mode shapes are the eigenvectors.

Hook otherwise checked: two equal masses on three identical springs have two normal modes, (1, 1) with k/m and (−1, 1) with 3k/m (SFU, source 21; Caltech, source 20), and any motion is a sum of them (MIT 8.03, source 19). What sets how fast each one goes is the eigenvalue.

In one breath checked against the research, with nothing overclaimed. Mixes of arrows reach a line, a plane or all of space (3Blue1Brown, sources 1 and 2). An arrow's numbers are amounts of the chosen basis arrows (sources 4 to 6). Lines and planes are a point plus directions, or a point and a normal (UConn, sources 7 and 8). Column space and null space decide how many answers a system has (MIT, sources 9 to 11). "Most matrices" having stretch-only directions is hedged rightly, since a shear lacks enough of them (source 16). Diagonalising turns 100 steps into one power (source 15). Tanks and masses split into modes, each with its own rate (sources 18, 19 and 21). Leaving out the mix of no arrows, which reaches only the origin, is a fair simplification.
